title: Skill Gap Analysis
text: A market-wide list of in-demand skills is not informative until it is compared against an existing sample person or persons. This analysis performs that comparison by measuring what employers in NAICS 523 ask for against records of what each member of the project team can actually do, and reports the distance between the two.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text: A market-wide list of in-demand skills is not informative until it is compared against an existing sample person or persons. This analysis performs that comparison by measuring what employers in NAICS 523 ask for against records of what each member of the project team can actually do, and reports the distance between the two.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Method
Demand is identified from 7,074 job postings, all of which list skills. The comparison skills come from an internal self-assessment: each team member rated their own proficiency on nine skill areas, on a five-point scale from beginner to expert. These rankings were then checked against those nine areas from the postings to determine which frequently requested skills fall outside them.
The gap for a given skill is the difference between the level the market requires and the level the individual holds. The required level was identified by how often the skill appears in postings.

Market Demand for Each Skill Area
The team searched SKILLS_NAME, the full skill list, rather than SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME to allow a more standard comparison as two of the selected areas- Communication and Financial Domain Knowledge- are not software and appear only in the full skills list. PANEL_PATH = Path("data/processed/career_market_panel.csv")
SKILL_FIELD = "SKILLS_NAME"

# Each skill area pattens

    "Python":                    r"\bpython\b",

    "Machine Learning":          r"machine learning|deep learning|predictive model|scikit|tensorflow|pytorch",
    "Cloud Computing":           r"cloud|\bazure\b|snowflake|databricks",
    "Communication":             r"communication|presentation|public speaking|storytelling",
    "AWS":                       r"\baws\b|amazon web services|amazon redshift|amazon s3",

    "Financial Domain Knowledge": r"financ|investment|securities|portfolio|accounting|asset management|risk management|trading|fixed income|derivative|valuation",
}
assert set(AREA_PATTERNS) == set(df_skills.columns), "Area names must match the ratings table"

panel = pd.read_csv(PANEL_PATH, usecols=[SKILL_FIELD], dtype=str)
n_postings = len(panel)

def clean_skill(name):
    return re.sub(r"\s*\([^)]*\)", "", name).strip().casefold()

skills_per_posting = (
    panel[SKILL_FIELD].fillna("[]")
    .apply(json.loads)
    .apply(lambda items: {clean_skill(x) for x in items if str(x).strip()})
)

# Match each distinct skill name once, then map postings to areas

    s: {a for a, p in AREA_PATTERNS.items() if re.search(p, s)} for s in skill_freq
}

    lambda skills: set().union(*(skill_to_areas[s] for s in skills))
)

Analysis
The team meets expectations in seven of the 9 areas Communication and dashboard/reporting but Financial domain is the one where every group member should focus on improving due it being the most demanded skill. Fuad and Katie are two levels behind while Jonathan is one level behind. The second skill to focus for the group would be SQL. In the group Fuad is below two levels and Jonathan is below one level, while Katie meets the expectations as illustrated by the learning chart. However, the team is doing well in Python, Machine Learning, Cloud Computing, AWS, and Git.


How to Close the Skill Gap
The way the team can close the gaps is a combination of peer learning and external courses. The following are some suggestions to start the improvement process:
External resources can be utilized such as Coursera learning paths, Udemycourses, and other online resources to fill in the gaps. The team can also consider pairing sessions where members with higher proficiency in certain areas can mentor others. For example, Katie can run short pairing sessions for Fuad and Jonathan in SQL. Jonathan can help with Financial Domain Knowledge by walking the team through topics such as financial analysis and risk management. However, no member meets the target in this area, so the whole group needs outside learning as well. We can set goals with a time frame, for example completing a Coursera course on finance or investments within the next three months.

title: Introduction
text: Students finishing an analytics degree face a market that looks uniform from the outside and is not. Job titles overlap, postings list long and inconsistent skill requirements, and the same title can mean very different work in different industries. A candidate deciding where to apply has no structured way to identify which industry rewards their current profile, which skills would raise their employment chances most, and what compensation and location trade-offs they are actually facing.

title: Introduction
text: Students finishing an analytics degree face a market that looks uniform from the outside and is not. Job titles overlap, postings list long and inconsistent skill requirements, and the same title can mean very different work in different industries. A candidate deciding where to apply has no structured way to identify which industry rewards their current profile, which skills would raise their employment chances most, and what compensation and location trade-offs they are actually facing.

title: Introduction
text:
Rationale
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment of data scientists to grow 35 percent between 2025 and 2035, far above the average for all occupations, with a 2025 median wage of $120,230 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026a)). Aggregate growth of this kind, however, tells an individual job seeker very little: it does not say which industry to target, which skills separate an interview from a rejection, or where an entry-level opening is realistically attainable.
Securities, commodity contracts, and other financial investments (NAICS 523) cover investment banks, brokerages, asset managers, and related financial-investment activities (U.S. Census Bureau (2022)). The subsector employed roughly 1.17 million people in the United States as of August 2026 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026b)). These firms employ analysts continuously for regulatory reporting, risk, performance measurement, and client analytics, which makes the segment large enough to analyse and specific enough to give actionable advice.
Prior research supports scoping the analysis to job postings. Content analyses of analytics job advertisements show that employer requirements cluster into distinct technical, analytical, and business-domain groups. The mix varies systematically by role and context (Verma et al. (2019)). Studies of entry-level analytics hiring similarly find a gap between what programs teach and what employers ask for in postings (Stanton and Stanton (2020)). A product that reads postings directly, rather than relying on generic career advice, will address that gap.

title: Introduction
text:
Scope Revision
The project originally anchored to NAICS 5221, Depository Credit Intermediation. Pulling that slice of postings returned only 59 results, with salary present on only 13, which would not support the compensation and skill-gap analysis planned for Modules 3 and 5. The team measured the adjacent industry codes and re-anchored to NAICS 523. The career pathway, the product question, and the underlying argument are unchanged; only the industry scope moved, and it remains inside Finance and Insurance. The evidence behind the decision is reported on the Data Preparation page.

title: Introduction
text:
Product Framing
The deliverable is a career evaluation product for a job seeker, not a general labor-market report. Every analysis in later modules is included only if it helps a student decide where to apply, what to learn next, and how to position themselves for BI/Data Analyst roles in NAICS 523.

title: Introduction
text:
Expected Findings

Postings will emphasise SQL, Excel, and BI tooling (Power BI, Tableau) more consistently than machine-learning frameworks.
Regulatory and domain vocabulary (risk, compliance, reporting) will appear frequently enough to act as a differentiator for candidates.
Remote openings will be less common than in the software sector, and concentrated in a small number of metropolitan areas.
The gap between market demand and a typical student profile will sit in domain knowledge and data governance rather than in programming.

These are expectations, not conclusions; Module 2 tests them against the MET Employability Career Match data; Module 3 retests them on the WRDS dataset supplied for this module.

title: Introduction
text:
What We Found
The expectations above were set before any data was pulled. Three modules later, three of the four can be checked against evidence on this site. They are reported here as they came out, including where we were wrong.
SQL and BI tooling over machine learning: confirmed, and by a wide margin. Across the nine skill areas measured on the Skill Gap Analysis page, dashboard and reporting tools appear in 22.3 percent of postings and SQL in 18.4 percent, against 2.8 percent for machine learning and 3.6 percent for cloud platforms. Reporting skills are asked for roughly eight times as often as modelling skills in this industry.
Domain vocabulary as a differentiator: confirmed, and it is the single strongest signal in the data. Financial and regulatory terminology appears in 66.7 percent of postings, the most demanded of the nine areas by a factor of nearly three over the runner-up. For a candidate, this is the finding with the most leverage: the vocabulary of the industry matters more than any individual tool.
Remote work rarer than in software: contradicted on flexibility, upheld on geography. On the 44 percent of postings that record a work arrangement, hybrid leads at 48 percent and fully remote at 32 percent, so four in five offer some flexibility — more, not less, than we expected. The second half of the prediction held: New York alone carries more postings than the next four cities combined, as shown on the Market Baseline page. We report the contradiction rather than revise the hypothesis after the fact.
The gap sits in domain knowledge rather than programming: partly confirmed. Domain knowledge is indeed where the shortfall is largest — no member of the team reaches the market target for it. But the prediction was wrong to exclude programming: SQL is the second-largest gap, and the data governance element we expected to measure never surfaced as a distinguishable category in the postings at all.

title: Market Baseline
text:
This is the current state of the market the product advises on: 7,074 postings for Business Intelligence and Data Analyst roles in NAICS 523, Securities, Commodity Contracts and Other Financial Investments, published on or after 1 September 2025.
Every figure below is drawn from data/processed/career_market_panel.csv. How that table was built, and where its gaps are, is documented on the Data Preparation page. Coverage varies sharply by field, so each chart states how many postings it is based on. Where a field proved unusable, it is indicated rather than reporting a number that is not supported.

title: Market Baseline
section: What The Occupation Codes Do— And Do Not— Tell Us
text:
What The Occupation Codes Do— And Do Not— Tell Us

Read this chart as a finding about the data, not about the market.
An occupational code is present on only 2,357 of 7,074 postings, 33 percent. Within that labeled third, Management Analysts account for 1,991 postings. But the coding itself does not survive inspection. Postings titled “Senior Financial Analyst, AWS GTM Finance” and “Sr Financial Analyst, Inbound Finance Insights” are coded as Models, Demonstrators, and Product Promoters — the third-largest occupation on the chart. On 2,165 postings the provider also overwrote the job title with the occupation name, so the title field on those rows describes a classification rather than a vacancy.
This is reported instead of being deleted because it justifies a design decision that runs through the whole project. The team’s role filter combines occupational codes with title keywords rather than trusting either alone, and this chart is the evidence for why. It is also a caution for anyone building on the same source: a market study that filtered on SOC codes here would silently describe the wrong population.
The practical consequence for a job seeker is narrower but real. Occupational classification in this industry is unreliable enough that filtering job boards by occupation category will both miss relevant roles and surface irrelevant ones.

title: Market Baseline
text:
How Titles Are Written

Rebuilt from the raw posting titles, the panel contains 4,000 distinct titles across 7,074 postings. The most common single title, “senior financial analyst”, appears 122 times — 1.7 percent of the panel.

The three most frequent titles together account for just 261 postings, under 4 percent of the market.
Titles here are effectively unique strings. The practical consequence for a candidate is that title-based job alerts are close to useless in this industry: a saved search for “Data Analyst” will miss over ninety percent of the relevant openings. Searching by skills and by employer returns far more of the real market.

title: Market Baseline
text:
What The Work Pays

Among the 1,741 postings (25 percent) that disclose pay, the median annual midpoint is $112,500, with the middle half falling between $87,500 and $141,500.
Postings that quote pay hourly or monthly are validated on their own scale rather than deleted as implausible, but they are not converted to annual figures, because the conversion requires an assumption about hours worked that the postings do not supply. This chart therefore covers the postings quoting annual pay.
Two cautions belong with the number. First, three postings in four say nothing about pay, and employers who publish ranges are not a random sample — pay-transparency laws apply in some states and not others, so the disclosed group skews toward those jurisdictions and toward larger employers. Second, this is the midpoint of a posted range, not an offer. Read it as an orientation for expectations, not a benchmark to negotiate against.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Where The Jobs Are

A usable state is recorded on 5,135 postings, 73 percent of the panel. New York leads with 726, followed by California (606), Texas (437), Florida (286) and Illinois (260).
That 73 percent is itself the product of cleaning. The raw field mixed full state names with two-letter codes, so New York appeared twice, and it also contained 1,202 postings labelled simply “United States” and 178 labelled “Remote” — a country and a work arrangement, neither of which is a place. Those were removed rather than counted.

At city level New York is the clear center with 783 postings, ahead of Washington (185), Chicago (136), Atlanta (107) and Seattle (106).
Securities and investments remains a concentrated industry geographically. New York alone holds more postings than the next four cities combined, which is a meaningful constraint for a candidate unwilling to relocate — and a meaningful argument for weighting remote-friendly employers.

title: Market Baseline
section: How Much Experience Is Asked For
text:
How Much Experience Is Asked For

A stated experience requirement survives on 1,702 postings, 24 percent of the panel. Among those, the median is three years and the middle half falls between two and five.
The coverage here is low for a reason worth recording. The raw field reported a requirement of zero years on 2,288 postings, but on 2,143 of them the stated maximum was exactly one year — a fixed “0 to 1” band attached to postings titled Senior Financial Analyst, Finance Manager and Accounting Manager. That is a provider default, not a market signal, and leaving it in produced a median of zero years. To prevent this, the placeholder band was removed and instead the smaller, reliable subset was reported.
On that subset, the market reads as mid-career but not closed: only 49 postings ask for less than a year, while 413 ask for five to six and 107 ask for ten or more. A student targeting this industry directly out of a program is competing for a narrow band of openings. The realistic paths are the small entry segment, adjacent industries with more junior demand, or roles where demonstrable skills substitute for years served. The Skill Gap Analysis page tests which skills most effectively close that distance.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Remote, Hybrid Or Onsite

A work arrangement is recorded on 3,126 postings, 44 percent of the panel. Among those, hybrid leads at 48 percent, fully remote at 32 percent and onsite at 20 percent.
This contradicts the expectation was set out in the Project Overview, where it was predicted that remote openings in finance would be rarer than in the software sector. On the labeled subset, four in five analytics postings in this industry offer some flexibility. The contradiction is reported rather than an adjustment to the hypothesis after the fact.
The caveat is the unlabelled majority. “Unknown” is shown as its own bar and never folded into “onsite”, because an unlabelled posting is an absence of information, not evidence of an office requirement.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Who Is Hiring

Before this section can say anything, the employer field needs cleaning. On 397 postings (6 percent) it holds an applicant-tracking hostname such as Eofe.fa.us2.oraclecloud.com instead of a company name, and on a further 229 (3 percent) it names a staffing agency or job aggregator rather than the firm doing the hiring. Three spellings of JPMorgan Chase were also being counted as three separate employers. All of these are flagged and set aside, which leaves 6,448 postings, 91 percent of the panel, with an identifiable employer.
On that subset the market is highly fragmented: 2,348 distinct employers. The largest, Amazon, accounts for 298 postings — 4.6 percent — followed by Citi at 2.2 percent, then U.S. Bank and JPMorgan Chase at 1.3 percent each. The top ten employers together hold 14 percent.
The strategic read changed once the employer names were cleaned. Before the merge, no firm appeared to hold more than a few percent and the only advice was to apply broadly. With the variants resolved a recognisable core emerges: Citi, U.S. Bank, JPMorgan Chase, PNC and State Street each run a steady analytics pipeline in this industry, and together with Amazon they account for roughly one posting in ten. Breadth still matters, because the other nine in ten are spread across 2,348 employers, but a candidate now has a short list worth following directly as well. Amazon’s position at the top is also a reminder that industry assignment follows the employer record rather than the specific business unit, so some postings sit in NAICS 523 for reasons that are not obvious from the company name.

title: Market Baseline
section: What This Means For The Product
text:
What This Means For The Product
Five things a candidate should take from this baseline:

Search by skills and employers, not by title or occupation. There are 4,000 distinct titles, the most common covers under two percent of the market, and the occupational codes are demonstrably wrong on a large share of postings.
Expect a mid-career market. Where a requirement is stated, the median is three years and fewer than one posting in thirty asks for less than a year.
Flexibility is available. Four in five labeled postings are remote or hybrid, which widens the geographic options considerably.
New York dominates, but not exclusively. It holds more postings than the next four cities combined; remote-friendly employers are the counterweight.
Treat salary figures as orientation. They come from the one posting in four that discloses pay.

The Skill Gap Analysis page turns these observations into a personal assessment: which skills separate the postings a given candidate can win from the ones they cannot, and what to learn first.

Figures and chart design by Katie Bowles. Field normalization and the Module 3 data-quality review by Fuad Babaiev.

title: Career Strategy and Recommendations
text: This is where the evidence becomes advice. The preceding pages establish what the market demands and where a candidate currently stands; this page answers the three questions a job seeker actually has: where to apply, what to learn next, and how to position themselves.

title: Career Strategy and Recommendations
text:
Process
The following recommendations are built from findings already on the site rather than from general career advice. The baseline established that job titles here are close to unique — 4,000 distinct titles across 7,074 postings, the most common covering under two percent — and that occupational codes are both too sparse and too often wrong to search by. Where an experience requirement is genuinely stated the median is three years, with fewer than one posting in thirty asking for less than a year. Four in five postings that record a work arrangement offer remote or hybrid work, and the employer side is fragmented enough that the largest single employer holds four percent of the market.

Be Specific
Based on the findings, the first recommendation is to be specific in a job search. The data shows that job titles are highly unique, which means that using broad or generic titles in a job application may not yield the best results. Instead, focus on the specific titles that align with your skills and experience.
The skills tied to higher pay include data architecture, advanced analytics, and technical accounting. More generic skills, such as problem solving, customer service, and financial analysis, are tied to lower pay.


Emphasize Machine Learning and Data Science
Based on the findings throughout this project, machine learning and data science are more likely to result in higher pay with less experience so applicants should explore aquiring or emphasiozing those skills.


Microsoft Office Does Not Standout
Microsoft Office and specifically Excel, are not standoput skills but establish a baseline for applicants. Excel is the most common skill but is associated with lower pay; it only shows in a small portion of the upper pay job postings.
A good alternative skill to acquire and add to be a standout applicant is a coding tool like Python and SQL to increase pay threshold.


Location Has a Lower Weight
Adding geography and remote status does not have a significant impact on job postings. The content of the job outweighs the location listed.


Filter Correctly
The majority of job findings indicate the postings are listed as entry level positions. So, for example, job seekers might rely too heavily on filter results that are removig viable jobs from appearing in their search.

title: Career Strategy and Recommendations
text:
Expectations and Actions
All of these findings indicate that applicants need to provide more focus, specific skills, and prioritize certain search features such as job level while discounting others such as location. All of these are simply recommendations to further an applicants success in finding jobs that they qualify for and ideally increasing the probability of a call back, however, applicants must do so truthfully. Falsifying a skill just to be more appealing on an application is not recommended by the team.
To successfully implement these recommendations, applicants and job seekers should:

Reevaluate their application materials and increase specificity
Emphasize unique skills that go beyond Microsoft Office
Acquire a new skill or certification in machine learning or Python
Apply a low weight to locations in listings
Filter more broadly keeping in mind that every application is different and filters may narrow the results too much

title: Evaluation Logic
text:
The other pages produce evidence. This one states the rules that turn that evidence into advice for one specific person, so a reader can judge the reasoning rather than take the conclusions on trust.
The product answers one question: given this market and this candidate, what should they do next? Getting from a market to a person takes six steps.

title: Evaluation Logic
text:
The other pages produce evidence. This one states the rules that turn that evidence into advice for one specific person, so a reader can judge the reasoning rather than take the conclusions on trust.
The product answers one question: given this market and this candidate, what should they do next? Getting from a market to a person takes six steps.

title: Evaluation Logic
text:
Step 1 — Define the market
Scope is fixed before anything is measured: NAICS 523, analytics roles, postings from 1 September 2025 onward. The rule for what counts as an analytics role combines occupational codes with title keywords, because on this source neither works alone. The Data Preparation page documents the filter and what it excludes.
Result: a panel of 7,074 postings.

title: Evaluation Logic
section: Step 2 — Measure what the market asks for
text:
Step 2 — Measure what the market asks for
Demand is the share of postings listing a skill. Nine skill areas, each defined by an explicit pattern over the skill field, measured on all 7,074 postings. No weighting by employer size or recency: a posting is a posting.

title: Evaluation Logic
section: Step 3 — Measure what the candidate has
text:
Step 3 — Measure what the candidate has
Self-assessment on the same nine areas, on a five-point scale from beginner to expert. This is the weakest link in the chain and we say so: it is self-reported, uncalibrated, and three people rating themselves is not a sample. It is a template for a candidate to fill in, not a measurement.

title: Evaluation Logic
section: Step 4 — Convert demand into a required level
text:
Step 4 — Convert demand into a required level
Market share is mapped to a target proficiency, so that demand and ability are expressed in the same units and can be subtracted. The cut-offs are our choice, not something the data dictates:



Share of postings
Target level

Because an area counts a posting if any of its skills appears, broad areas score higher shares than narrow ones. Targets should be read with that in mind.

title: Evaluation Logic
section: Step 5 — Compute the gap and order the work
text:
Step 5 — Compute the gap and order the work
The gap is the target minus the level held, floored at zero. Learning priority is the gap weighted by the area’s market share, so closing a small gap in a heavily demanded area beats closing a large gap in a rare one. The Skill Gap Analysis page applies this and produces a per-person learning order.

title: Evaluation Logic
section: Step 6 — Refuse what the data cannot support
text:
Step 6 — Refuse what the data cannot support
The same discipline runs through every page. Where the evidence will not carry a conclusion, we report the limit instead of the conclusion:

Occupation codes are present on a third of postings and misclassify senior finance roles where present, so no finding rests on them.
Missing work arrangement is never read as “onsite”. Absence of information is not information.
A provider placeholder of 0-to-1 years attached to senior postings was removed rather than averaged in, which cut usable experience data from 56 percent to 24 percent and moved the median from zero years to three.
Model coefficients are reported only for skills with at least 30 supporting postings, and only where the conditional estimate and the raw share agree.

title: Evaluation Logic
text:
Where the Models Fit
Steps 1 to 5 describe a candidate against the market. The Predictive Modeling page asks the harder question — which skills actually separate a better opportunity from a worse one — and answers it two ways: by pay, with a regression, and by reachability, with a classifier. Their output feeds the Career Strategy page, where the gap analysis and the models combine into specific actions.

title: Evaluation Logic
section: What This Product Does Not Do
text:
What This Product Does Not Do
It does not predict whether an individual will be hired. It does not price a particular job. It does not rank employers by anything other than posting volume. And because every skill measure comes from job advertisements, it describes what employers write down, which is not the same as what they actually require.

title: Data Preparation
text: Every figure on the analysis pages comes from one table. This page documents how that table was built: what was pulled, what was kept, what was removed, and what was repaired. Anyone reading the conclusions should be able to judge how much weight the evidence can carry.

The date window keeps the analysis current: the source spans postings back to 2014, and hiring requirements from a decade ago describe a market the target user is not applying into. In practice the window costs little — only 192 in-scope postings predate it.

Why this industry, and why a three-digit code
Module 1 anchored the project to NAICS 5221, Depository Credit Intermediation. That code returned 59 postings in total, too few to support compensation or skill-gap analysis, and lead to the analysis being re-anchored to NAICS 523 after measuring the neighbouring codes. NAICS 523 accounts for roughly two-thirds of all analytics postings within Finance and Insurance, so it is where the market actually is.
The assignment asks for four- or six-digit codes where possible. The earlier source carried no four-digit granularity beneath 523; this dataset does expose NAICS4 through NAICS6, and those columns are retained in the panel for finer analysis, but 523 remains the scope boundary so that the project stays comparable across modules.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Role Definition
The assignment allows title keywords, SOC or O*NET mappings, skills logic, or a combination, provided the choice is explained. For this analysis, the team uses a combination, and this dataset makes the case stronger than before: occupation codes are present on only a third of postings, so an occupation-only filter would discard two postings in three unseen.
A posting is kept when either condition holds:

its SOC occupation matches one of: data scientist, database architect, statistician, mathematician, operations research, market research analyst, financial and investment analyst, credit analyst, management analyst
or its title contains one of: analyst, analytics, data, business intelligence, BI, reporting, SQL, data science, machine learning

Information-security roles are then removed. They match the word “analyst” but belong to a different career pathway, and including them would distort the skill profile the product reports.

title: Data Preparation
text:
Cleaning Decisions
Cleaning stays conservative. Where a value is implausible a blank is inserted into that field rather than an assumed a replacement, and where a whole posting is questionable it is recorded as a gap. Deleting rows narrows the sample; blanking one field costs only that field.
The rules below were written for Module 2 by Katie Bowles and carried over unchanged; only the column names differ, and the salary handling is extended because this dataset quotes pay in several periods.
Duplicates. Deduplicated on the posting identifier. None remained.
Rows missing essentials. A posting is dropped if it has no identifier, title, employer or publication date. After the date filter, none failed this test.
Dates. Parsed to a single format. Where an expiry date preceded the publication date the expiry would be blanked, since one of the two must be wrong and it cannot be determined which is incorrect; no postings were affected.
Salary. The provider’s SALARY column turned out to be a free-text summary whose value is an empty placeholder on most rows, so it is kept for reference but never used as a figure. The usable numbers are the structured range, and that range is quoted in different periods — 1,751 annual, 315 hourly, 18 monthly. Each is validated against bounds appropriate to its own period rather than a single annual rule, which had been silently deleting hourly rates as “implausible”. Reversed ranges are swapped, zeros treated as missing, and 20 rows were cleared as out of range across all periods.
Hourly and monthly rates are kept in their own columns and are not converted to annual figures, because the conversion requires an assumption about hours worked that the postings do not supply. ANNUAL_SALARY_MID — the midpoint of the annual range — is the field used for salary analysis, and it is populated on 1,741 postings.
Experience and education. Taken directly from the provider’s coded fields. Unlike the earlier panel these are not team estimates, so no parsing decisions were needed.
Skills. Arrive as arrays and are stored as JSON-style list strings — for example ["Microsoft Excel", "SQL (Programming Language)"] — across four fields: all skills, named software, specialised skills and transferable skills, plus certifications. Names are not yet normalised, so casing and synonyms remain distinct; that normalisation belongs to the skill-gap work, where it has an analytical purpose. Code reading these fields must parse the list rather than splitting on a delimiter.
Remote status. Never inferred, and category labels are normalised because the source spells the same category two ways. A posting with no remote label is an absence of information, not evidence of an office requirement.
Location. Text fields trimmed of stray whitespace. This dataset carries no coordinates, so the latitude and longitude check from the earlier pipeline does not apply; geography is carried by state, city and metropolitan area.
Types. Every column is cast explicitly — dates, booleans, numbers and categories — so later analysis cannot silently treat a number as text.

Field Normalization
Integration testing in Module 3 exposed four defects that coverage statistics alone do not reveal. Each repair is written to a separate column, so the provider’s original value stays auditable.
The job title is overwritten on part of the panel. On 2,165 postings — 31 percent — TITLE_NAME holds the occupation name instead of the advertised title, so a vacancy posted as “Sr Financial Analyst, AWS GTM Finance” reads simply as “Management Analysts”. Counting titles from that field produced an apparent leading title of “management analysts” with 1,991 postings, which is an artifact of the coding and not a fact about the market. TITLE_CLEAN is rebuilt from the raw title text instead, raising the number of distinct titles from 2,396 to 4,000.
Occupational coding is wrong on identifiable rows, not merely sparse. Several postings titled Senior Financial Analyst are coded as Models, Demonstrators, and Product Promoters. The field is kept and the defect reported rather than deleted, because it is the direct justification for defining roles by title as well as by code.
The state field is not only a state field. It mixes full names with two-letter codes, so New York appeared twice — as “New York” (514) and as “NY” (212) — and it carries 1,202 postings labelled “United States” and 178 labeled “Remote”, a country and a work arrangement. STATE_CLEAN expands the codes and discards the non-geographic values, which lowers real coverage from an apparent 92 percent to an honest 73 percent.
Two fields encode “missing” as a value. REMOTE_TYPE_NAME carries a literal “Unknown” on 1,442 postings alongside 2,506 true nulls, and spells the office category both “Onsite” and “On-site”; REMOTE_CLEAN merges the spellings and treats “Unknown” as missing, leaving 44 percent labelled. MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE reports zero years on 2,288 postings, but on 2,143 of them the stated maximum is exactly one — a fixed “0 to 1” band attached to postings titled Senior Financial Analyst, Finance Manager and Accounting Manager. That is a provider default, and left in place it produced a median requirement of zero years across the panel. MIN_YEARS_EXP_CLEAN removes the band, leaving 1,702 postings with a stated requirement and a median of three years.
Several headline numbers fall as a result. That is the intended outcome: the higher figures counted placeholders as data.
A fifth defect surfaced in Module 5, in the employer field. On 397 postings it holds an applicant-tracking hostname rather than a company name, on 229 it names a staffing agency or job aggregator rather than the hiring firm, and one employer appeared under three spellings. The provider’s own COMPANY_IS_STAFFING flag cannot be used to find these: it is set on 93 of 7,074 rows and contradicts itself, marking TD as staffing while giving JPMorgan Chase both values. EMPLOYER_CLEAN, EMPLOYER_UNIDENTIFIED and IS_AGENCY record the repair without dropping any rows, so employer concentration is measured on the 6,448 postings where a hiring firm can actually be identified.

Four limitations shape how the analysis pages should be read.
Salary is disclosed on one posting in four. Employers who publish pay ranges are not a random sample — pay-transparency law applies in some states and not others — so the disclosed group likely skews toward those jurisdictions and toward larger employers. Every salary figure in this project describes that subset, not the market.
Occupation codes are sparse and partly wrong. Only a third of postings carry a SOC occupation, and within that third the classification misassigns senior finance roles badly enough to be caught by eye. Any breakdown by occupation describes the coded third, and comparisons between occupations are ratios within that subset rather than counts of the whole market.
Titles are dependable, classifications are not. Raw title text is present on every posting and is what is counted. Provider-normalised titles and occupation codes are used only where the analysis is explicitly about data quality.
Experience survives on one posting in four. The provider supplies a value more often than that, but most of the additional rows carry a placeholder band rather than a requirement. It is a reliable number where present, but absence is common and should not be read as “no experience required”.
Against that, geography and skills are close to complete, which means the location analysis and the skill-gap work — the parts the product most depends on — rest on much firmer ground than the compensation analysis does.

title: Career Evaluation Product — Group 1
text:
Product Question

Which skills, locations, and role variants give an early-career candidate the strongest entry into Business Intelligence / Data Analyst roles at U.S. securities and investment firms (NAICS 523), and which skills are missing from a current student profile?

title: Career Evaluation Product — Group 1
text:
Why This Industry
Securities, commodity contracts, and other financial investment activities (NAICS 523) run continuous reporting, risk, performance-attribution, and client-analytics functions that are staffed by business intelligence and data analyst roles rather than by research scientists. Because investment analytics is shaped by regulatory reporting and legacy data infrastructure, its skill profile differs from the software sector — SQL, data governance, and domain knowledge often matter as much as machine-learning depth. The subsector is also the single largest source of analytics postings within Finance and Insurance in the data source, which makes the scope both coherent and large enough to support a decision-oriented product.

title: Career Evaluation Product — Group 1
text:
Scope Revision
Module 1 anchored the project to NAICS 5221, Depository Credit Intermediation. When pulled in Module 2, the data returned 59 postings in total, of which 13 carried salary information — too thin to support the planned skill-gap and compensation analysis later in the project. Because of that the team measured the neighbouring industry codes and moved the anchor to NAICS 523, which keeps the project inside Finance and Insurance while providing 15,176 postings, of which 6,199 matched our career pathway. Module 3 rebuilt the panel from the supplied WRDS dataset on the same scope: 24,914 postings in NAICS 523 and 7,074 after the role filter. The measurement and the filter rule are documented on the Data Preparation page.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
The earlier pages describe what the market looks like. This page asks a narrower question, the one Module 5 was built around: which skills most strongly distinguish stronger opportunities from weaker ones?
“Stronger” is defined two ways, because a job seeker cares about two different things. A stronger posting pays more, and a stronger posting is one they can realistically get. Each definition gets its own model.
Both models read the same input: a binary indicator for each of the 179 skills that appear in at least one percent of the panel, built once in notebooks/30_build_features.py. Postings list a median of ten skills each, drawn from 3,327 distinct names.






Note



The skill field is stored as a JSON list, not as delimited text. Splitting it on a separator silently collapses an entire posting into a single skill, which produces plausible-looking but meaningless counts. The feature builder parses it.

title: Predictive Modeling
section: Track 1 — Regression: What Skills Are Worth
text:
Track 1 — Regression: What Skills Are Worth

What was modeled
The natural logarithm of the annual salary midpoint, predicted from the skills a posting lists. Pay is heavily right-skewed in this panel, from $25,000 to $696,000 against a median of $112,500, so a model on the raw figure would chase a handful of very large ranges. Working in logs also makes each coefficient readable as an approximate percentage effect on pay.
Two specifications were fitted. The first uses skills alone. The second adds the ten largest states and the work arrangement as controls, so that the skill effects can be separated from the simple fact that some cities pay more.


Why it matters for a job seeker
A candidate choosing what to learn next is making an investment decision. Knowing which skills sit in better-paid postings turns that choice from guesswork into something measurable.


What variables were used
179 binary skill indicators, plus 13 geography and work-arrangement controls in the second specification. Fitted on the 1,741 postings (25 percent of the panel) that disclose pay, with ridge regularisation and the penalty chosen by cross-validation.


How performance was evaluated
A quarter of the postings were held out and never used in fitting. Results are reported on that held-out set and confirmed with five-fold cross-validation.

Two things stand out. The skill mix explains roughly a third of the variation in pay, which is substantial for a model that reads nothing but a list of keywords. And adding geography barely moves the result — 0.366 to 0.373. In this industry, what the job asks for matters more than where it is.


What the result means in practical career terms

Coefficients are reported only for the 107 skills appearing in at least 30 of the salaried postings; 72 rarer skills were estimated but are not shown, because a coefficient fitted on a handful of rows is noise rather than a finding.
Skills associated with higher pay: advanced analytics (+22%), executive leadership (+20%), data architecture (+19%), technical accounting (+18%), public accounting (+17%), data science (+17%), fixed income (+15%), capital markets (+15%).
Skills associated with lower pay: problem solving (−28%), financial data (−19%), customer service (−16%), organizational skills (−12%), Microsoft Office (−12%), financial analysis (−9%), Microsoft Excel (−9%), Power BI (−9%).
The pattern is not “technical versus non-technical”. It is specific versus generic. Compare the pairs: “financial analysis” costs 9 percent, while “fixed income” and “capital markets” each add 15. “Problem solving” costs 28 percent, while “data architecture” adds 19. The same holds for tools — Microsoft Excel appears in 779 of the salaried postings and is associated with lower pay, while Power BI, a real BI tool, carries no premium either.

The honest limit: two thirds of the variation in pay remains unexplained, and the average error is still $28,500. This model narrows a guess; it does not price a job.

title: Predictive Modeling
section: Track 2 — Classification: Which Postings Are Reachable
text:
Track 2 — Classification: Which Postings Are Reachable

What was modeled
Whether a posting is entry level or advanced, predicted from its skills. Postings stating a requirement of two years or less are labelled entry level; the rest are advanced. The split is 542 entry against 1,160 advanced, so the classes are imbalanced and the model was fitted with balanced class weights.


Why it matters for a job seeker
The Market Baseline established that this is a mid-career market: where a requirement is stated at all, the median is three years. A student leaving a programme is competing for the smaller share. A model that can read seniority from the skill list lets them filter a job board down to the postings actually worth an application.


What variables were used
The same 179 skill indicators, fitted on the 1,702 postings (24 percent) that state an experience requirement, with logistic regression and the penalty chosen by cross-validation.


How performance was evaluated
The same held-out quarter, judged on precision and recall for each class rather than on accuracy alone.

The model does not beat the baseline on accuracy, and we report that plainly. It is marginally worse, 0.678 against 0.681. But accuracy is the wrong measure here. The baseline reaches 68 percent by calling every posting advanced, which means it identifies zero of the openings a student could apply to. The model finds 91 of 136. For a product whose job is to say “apply here”, that difference is the entire value, and an AUC of 0.741 confirms the signal is real rather than noise.
The cost is visible in the matrix: 45 entry-level postings were missed, and 92 advanced postings were wrongly flagged as reachable. A candidate using this filter will waste some applications. That is the better error to make — a wasted application costs an hour, a missed opening costs the job.


What the result means in practical career terms

Two skills separate completely — every posting listing data architecture (52 postings, 100 percent advanced) and treasury management (57 postings, 98 percent) falls on the senior side. For these the direction is certain but the magnitude is an artifact, so only the direction is reported.
Among the rest, the markers of a senior posting are consistently specific: data governance (97 percent advanced), information technology (97 percent), bank secrecy act (98 percent), technical accounting (88 percent), general ledger (85 percent), risk analytics (83 percent).
The entry-level signal is much weaker, and this is itself a finding. Against a base rate of 68 percent advanced, only a few skills sit meaningfully below it: research (28 percent advanced), employee benefits (44 percent), business development (47 percent), data analysis tools (50 percent). Most of the remaining “entry markers” sit within a few points of the base rate. Postings announce seniority clearly; they do not announce accessibility.






WarningA caution on reading coefficients



A logistic coefficient is conditional on every other skill in the posting; the raw share of advanced postings is not. For 21 of the 107 skills the two disagree — “sales” carries the strongest entry-level coefficient in the model, yet 69 percent of postings listing it are advanced, slightly above the base rate. Where the two measures conflict, the effect is a product of correlation between skills and is not reported here as a property of the skill. Only skills where both point the same way appear in the lists above.

title: Predictive Modeling
section: What The Two Models Say Together
text:
What The Two Models Say Together
They agree, and the agreement is the finding.
Specificity is what the market pays for and promotes on. Across both models the same division appears: named capabilities — data architecture, data governance, technical accounting, fixed income, capital markets, bank secrecy act — sit in the well-paid and senior postings. Generic descriptors — problem solving, analytical skills, organizational skills, business acumen — sit in the cheap and junior ones. A candidate writing a CV should take this literally: “experienced with financial analysis” is the phrasing of a $90,000 posting, “fixed income attribution” is the phrasing of a $140,000 one.
There is one skill set that pays well without demanding years. Machine learning appears in 7.6 percent of top-quartile postings and in none of the bottom quartile, yet on the seniority split it sits at the base rate — 67 percent advanced against 68 percent overall. The same broadly holds for data science. For a student leaving a programme, that combination is the clearest point of leverage in this data: a skill that raises the pay a posting offers without raising the experience it demands.
Excel is the floor, not the ladder. It appears in 779 of the 1,741 salaried postings, more than any other skill, and is associated with lower pay in the model and with the bottom quartile in the raw comparison. It is necessary and it is not an advantage.
These three findings feed the Career Strategy page, where they become specific actions.

title: Predictive Modeling
text:
Limitations
Both models describe disclosed subsets. Pay is stated on 25 percent of the panel and experience on 24 percent, and neither group is a random sample — pay-transparency law varies by state, and employers who state requirements may differ systematically from those who do not. Every number here describes the postings that told us, not the market.
Association is not causation. Listing Python does not cause a posting to pay more. Python marks a different kind of role, and the role carries the pay. The practical reading is about which postings to target, not about what adding a line to a CV will do on its own.
The feature set is deliberately narrow. Only skills are used, because the question was about skills. Employer, title seniority and city are not in the model, which is why the regression leaves two thirds of the variation unexplained.
Skill names are the provider’s. They are normalised for case and bracketed qualifiers but not for synonyms, so closely related names are counted separately.
